output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for waiting, Doctor. You have known the household a long time.

DR VAUTHIER: Thirty years, Inspector. I attended Aurèle through his gout and his bad winters, and I sat with his brother Jules in his last illness, in eighteen eighty-nine. Aurèle never quite forgave me for not curing Jules. I doubt he forgave anyone anything.

MATTHEY: Tell me about dinner.

DR VAUTHIER: When the temple struck nine, Aurèle asked us all to show our watches, as he does every year. He has his little judgements for each of us. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. He told me so, and I told him I had never been on time for anything in my life except a bill.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I played piquet in the salon. Madame is the better player, though she will never admit it. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch, when I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. Madame began to play the piano as I went out.

MATTHEY: What did she play?

DR VAUTHIER: Chopin. She plays Chopin when she is thinking about something she will not discuss. I did not listen closely. I was looking for my cigars.

MATTHEY: And when you came back?

DR VAUTHIER: She had stopped playing, and we went on with our game.

MATTHEY: Did you notice the time while you played?

DR VAUTHIER: When the temple struck ten during our game, I noticed the salon clock showed five minutes to ten, and I remarked on it to Madame.

MATTHEY: Which clock is that?

DR VAUTHIER: The marble mantel clock. It is the one Odile has always kept by the piano.

MATTHEY: You have seen the body, Doctor. What can you tell me of it?

DR VAUTHIER: A blow to the back of the head, struck from behind. It was a heavy blow, and I would say death was very quick. He would not have known much about it. That is all a physician can say, and I have said it in my statement.

MATTHEY: Can you tell me the hour of his death?

DR VAUTHIER: No, Inspector, and I will not guess one for you. A man struck down is not a clock. I can tell you how he died, not when the last of his breath left him, and I would not wish to mislead your men with a number I cannot support.

MATTHEY: The regulator in the atelier. Did it mean anything to him?

DR VAUTHIER: It was the thing he loved best after his wife and his watches, and not always in that order. It stopped with its master. I say that as a friend and not as a physician.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you wish to add?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that I have been wanting a cigar since dinner, and that your questions have reminded me of a tag Aurèle liked to quote. *Tempus edax rerum*, Inspector. Time devours all things, and watches most of all.
